set_up: Develop enough early bodies to attack profitably.
decision: If another creature does not improve your next attack then keep it in hand to rebuild after a sweeper.
finish: Use a team boost or evasion when it turns a crowded board into a decisive attack.
role_note: Early bodies put opponents on a clock. Making tokens does not by itself make the deck a combo deck.
combat_position: You have five tokens. One defender can eat a token, but an attack trigger makes a replacement.
combat_choice: Compare the damage and trigger with the blockers you will need afterward. Send the profitable attackers; the token count is not a reason to send all five.

set_up: Choose an attacker that can get through. Budget for attaching Equipment as well as casting it.
decision: Before adding more power ask whether protection or evasion would buy an extra hit instead.
finish: Count the attacks you need against one player. Track commander combat damage separately from ordinary damage.
role_note: The enhanced attacker is the clock. Protecting it serves the attack plan rather than making the deck control.
combat_position: One opponent is closest to lethal commander damage but has a blocker. Another player is open.
combat_choice: Count hits against each player separately. Spend evasion if it removes a full attack from the clock; otherwise consider the open player and keep protection available.

set_up: Land an attacker before spending cards to slow someone down.
decision: Return a blocker to hand before combat if the attack you gain matters. Without an attacker that same spell may only help the other players.
finish: Keep attacking while the defender spends mana replaying cards. Save your last answer for what would stop the decisive hit.
role_note: Tempo is aggro-control: the threat makes each turn matter, and temporary disruption buys that threat another attack.
combat_position: Your attacker draws a card when it hits a player. One opponent has a blocker; another may be open.
combat_choice: Check the open attack first. Bounce the blocker if hitting that defender matters enough to spend the spell. Without a useful attack, their lost tempo may benefit someone else.

set_up: Put a creature on the board that can trade early and still generate value later.
decision: Against a faster deck trade to stay alive. Against a slower engine deploy pressure before it takes over.
finish: Once you're ahead on board start attacking instead of exchanging cards indefinitely.
role_note: Midrange can defend against a faster start or become the aggressor against a slower engine. The table determines its role.
combat_position: Your best attacker could pressure the player drawing extra cards, but the next player has a larger board.
combat_choice: If you can survive the return attack, pressure the slower engine now. If not, keep the blocker and take the exchange that stabilizes you.

set_up: Pass with enough mana for an answer and an instant-speed use for that mana if no answer is needed.
decision: Let a spell resolve if it does not threaten your plan. Draw cards on the last opponent's end step if your mana is still free.
finish: Deploy a threat when you can protect it. Keep attacking while reserving answers for plays that change the race.
role_note: Permission buys time. Some builds protect a decisive interaction; others win with a threat while continuing to hold answers.
combat_position: A blocker could trade with your only threat. You can bounce it now, but that uses the mana for your counterspell.
combat_choice: Take a free attack elsewhere or pass. Clearing a blocker is worthwhile when the hit matters more than the opposing spell you may need to stop.

set_up: Identify what you can keep on the battlefield through your own sweeper.
decision: Decide whether to sweep now or take another hit. Avoid committing the threat you need to win just before the reset.
finish: Use the permanent that survived or deploy a threat while opponents are rebuilding.
role_note: Board resets and proactive permanents establish control. Winning with an attacker later does not make early aggression the plan.
combat_position: You intend to sweep after combat. An opponent can trade for your attacker, but their potential crack-back would otherwise be lethal.
combat_choice: If the sweep is secure, get the damage or trade before the reset. If the sweep could be stopped, weigh keeping your blocker against that risk.

set_up: Establish a source of pressure or resources that will still function under your restriction.
decision: Check who is actually slowed before playing the restriction. An opponent already ahead on board may benefit most.
finish: Attack or grow your board while opponents are constrained. The restriction buys time but does not win by itself.
role_note: Restrictions control opponents' options. Aggro-stax adds an early attacker so opponents lose time and life together.
combat_position: Your attack tax slows two opponents, but the third has enough mana to pay it. Your only attacker is also a good blocker.
combat_choice: Pressure a player who cannot race you, but leave a defense against the one who can. The tax is useful only if you make progress under it.

set_up: Find three distinct jobs: creatures you can spare; a way to sacrifice them; a reward when they die.
decision: Against removal you can often sacrifice the threatened creature in response. Check the outlet cost and whether the payoff counts tokens.
finish: Turn a renewable supply of bodies into repeated life loss. Check whether the payoff reaches one opponent or each opponent.
role_note: Some sacrifice decks attack with disposable bodies; others assemble an outlet, renewable material, and a payoff. A death trigger alone is not a combo finish.
combat_position: A token can attack into a larger blocker. You have a sacrifice outlet and a payoff that rewards that token dying.
combat_choice: Let the defender choose blocks before deciding whether to sacrifice it. Compare the death reward with dealing combat damage or keeping the token to block next turn.

set_up: Get a useful creature into your graveyard with a way to return it.
decision: Choose the target for what happens as it enters or survives a turn. A cast trigger will not fire just because the creature returns.
finish: Bring back the threat that can end this game rather than the one with the highest mana value.
role_note: A discard-and-return sequence can deliver a threat early, fuel attacks, or repeatedly bring back a creature that controls the board.
combat_position: You can return a huge creature without haste or a smaller creature whose entry removes a blocker. You already have attackers.
combat_choice: Count the damage the smaller creature opens up now. Take the larger threat if its defense or next attack matters more.

set_up: Work backward from the play you want to make early. Check the colors as well as the total mana.
decision: If another mana source does not bring that play forward decide whether to find a payoff or defend yourself instead.
finish: Spend the mana on a threat or repeatable activation that changes the board before the table can catch up.
role_note: Extra mana is the means, not the role: it can accelerate attackers, pay for a combo, or fund resets and repeated answers.
combat_position: Your mana creature can attack for one, but tapping it for mana after combat would let you cast a threat this turn.
combat_choice: Keep it back if the extra mana advances the threat by a turn. Attack if the damage matters and your lands can already pay for the follow-up.

set_up: Develop a permanent that rewards casting spells before using your cheapest spells.
decision: Sequence a draw spell first if it could change your next play. Save interaction when spending it would leave the chain exposed.
finish: Use the spell rewards your deck actually makes: attack with the tokens or finish with accumulated damage.
role_note: Spell rewards can make attackers, fuel a decisive spell chain, or replenish a control deck's answers.
combat_position: A cheap instant makes a token through your payoff. You have attackers, and another player may need answering before your next turn.
combat_choice: A new token without haste cannot join this attack. Cast now only for a benefit you can use now; otherwise preserve the option to interact.

set_up: Identify the pieces and what the sequence produces. Find the missing function rather than a duplicate of one you already have.
decision: Check every cost and likely interruption before committing. Waiting is useful only if it improves the next attempt.
finish: Demonstrate how the output wins. Making unlimited mana still requires something that can spend it.
role_note: The interaction is central. Combat pressure can buy an opening, or control can protect the assembly turn.
combat_position: A creature you need to start your combo could attack for two, but an opponent has a profitable block.
combat_choice: Keep the piece safe unless the attack changes the race. You need not spend your removal on a blocker that does not stop the combo.

set_up: Pair a creature with a useful entry effect and a way to use that effect again.
decision: Choose between protecting a creature and repeating its ability. Check when it returns before counting on it to block.
finish: Repeat the effect that clears an attack or builds a winning board rather than blinking for value indefinitely.
role_note: Reusing an entry effect may repeatedly answer threats. It becomes a combo route when a specific sequence produces a decisive result.
combat_position: You can blink your tapped attacker after combat. It can draw a card on entry, but your blink spell is also your protection against removal.
combat_choice: Attack if the exchange is safe. Blink afterward if the card or a fresh blocker matters; keep the spell if losing that creature would break your engine.

set_up: Put down artifacts that do useful work before the payoff arrives.
decision: An artifact you spend or sacrifice now may be the one you need for mana later. Work out both turns before using it.
finish: Convert the artifacts into the output your deck supports: attacking power or a repeatable resource with a winning outlet.
role_note: Artifacts can be an attacking army, components in a resource loop, or reusable answers. Their shared type does not pick the role.
combat_position: Your artifact creature can attack or tap for mana to activate a second artifact during the next player's turn.
combat_choice: Compare the actual hit with what the activation prevents or produces. Do not count the same tapped creature as both an attacker and an unused mana source.

set_up: Pair an enchantment reward with cheap enchantments you would still want to play on their own.
decision: If you can do so safely play the draw engine first. Check whether it rewards casting an enchantment or its entry.
finish: Use the extra cards to build an evasive attacker or a threatening board. Drawing the next enchantment is not itself a finish.
role_note: Auras can support an attacker, linked enchantments can combine for a finish, or enchantment-based answers can sustain control.
combat_position: Before combat you can cast an Aura for evasion and trigger your draw effect. The defender still has mana open.
combat_choice: Cast it before attacks if evasion buys a meaningful hit. If another opponent is open, attack there and avoid risking both the Aura and its target for no extra damage.

set_up: Pair a land-entry reward with ways to find or replay lands.
decision: Consider playing the payoff before your land for the turn. A land found into hand is not an extra land play.
finish: Turn repeated land entries into an army or damage rather than just building a larger mana base.
role_note: Land entries can grow attackers, feed a repeatable sequence, or support control through utility lands. Extra land drops alone do not choose a role.
combat_position: Your attacker grows when a land enters. You can make your normal land play now or save a land-search activation until after blocks.
combat_choice: Make the land play before combat if it improves the attack. Save the activation when it can change a trade, and check that it puts a land onto the battlefield rather than into hand.

set_up: Keep track of which threats and answers your search cards can find.
decision: Count the cost of finding the card and playing it. Take the less expensive answer if the ideal one would arrive too late.
finish: Once the board is safe search for the threat that ends the game instead of another situational answer.
role_note: Searching is a means to an end: one build finds an answer for each board, another finds pieces for a winning interaction.
combat_position: You can search for a creature that grants evasion, but casting it before combat would take the rest of your mana.
combat_choice: Count the search and casting costs together. Find the evasion piece if this attack is decisive; otherwise keep access to the answer you may need on the next turn.

set_up: Identify what the shared creature type lets your creatures do together: produce mana or draw cards or attack for more.
decision: Choose whether another creature or a reward for creatures already in play makes the bigger difference this turn.
finish: Time the shared boost or use the type-based engine to power a finisher. A creature count alone does not tell you when to attack.
role_note: A shared type can scale attacks, supply the mana for a combo, or reward holding up interaction. The particular type payoff decides.
combat_position: Your lord boosts several attackers, but attacking with it would expose it to a first-strike blocker.
combat_choice: Check the combat math without the bonus. Leave the lord back if losing it before ordinary damage would turn favorable attacks into trades.

set_up: Establish a repeatable source of damage or life loss and note which players it affects.
decision: Use a burst on a creature if that keeps you alive for more triggers. Otherwise count whether saving it will finish an opponent.
finish: Combine the remaining burst with repeatable damage. Check your own life total before relying on a symmetrical effect.
role_note: Life-total pressure sets the clock. Some group-slug builds also restrict or punish opposing actions while they manage the race.
combat_position: A burn spell can hit a defender or remove a blocker that would otherwise stop your attacker for several turns.
combat_choice: Compare direct damage with the attacks removal actually unlocks. If another opponent can take the hit this turn, keeping the burn spell may do more.

set_up: Identify who benefits most from the resources you offer and what you get even without a deal.
decision: Offer selective help when it deals with a shared danger. Avoid feeding the player who can win first with extra cards.
finish: Use the time you gained to build your own winning position rather than relying on opponents to honor a future deal.
role_note: Selective protection and incentives can steer attacks and buy time. Helping the table is not itself control or a way to win.
combat_position: One opponent offers not to attack you if you swing at the player with the largest board. That attack would leave you without a blocker.
combat_choice: Judge the board if the deal falls through. Take the attack only if the pressure or the time it buys is worth exposing yourself to the rest of the table.

set_up: Plan land colors around the sequence of efficient attackers you want to cast on the first turns.
decision: Clear a blocker if doing so buys more damage than adding your next threat. Concentrate pressure where your attacks still matter.
finish: Use evasion or direct damage to finish a weakened opponent when larger creatures start to stall combat.
role_note: Efficient creatures and removal keep the pressure on from the opening turns. The removal is there to keep attacks profitable.
combat_position: Two early attackers can get past one big blocker if you spend a removal spell. You could instead add a third attacker after combat.
combat_choice: Remove the blocker if the extra damage now puts that player within reach. If it only trades a spell for a small hit, develop the board or attack an open opponent.

set_up: Make an early play that stands on its own while setting up a way to replenish threats.
decision: Choose a threat over another answer if an opponent's engine will win a long game. Keep an independent follow-up in reserve.
finish: Use the advantage you built to present consecutive threats that the table cannot all answer.
role_note: Independent threats and answers let a deck press or defend. A pile of strong cards does not imply a combo without a specific interaction.
combat_position: You have the best attacker and a second threat in hand. A different player's draw engine will take over if everyone waits.
combat_choice: Attack the engine player if the return attack is manageable. Develop the second threat only if the extra pressure is worth having less to rebuild with.
